prompt: A report query uses `JSON_TABLE`. It runs on Ana's laptop and fails with a syntax error on the staging server. Nobody edited the query. What is the most likely difference?

choices.text: Staging is on PostgreSQL 16, a release before that feature
choices.why: Right. 17 added it, so the same text is valid SQL on one machine and a syntax error on the other.

choices.text: The server's copy of the query was corrupted on its way from the repository
choices.why: The text is identical on both machines; what differs is the database reading it.

choices.text: Syntax errors depend on the operating system of the client that sends the query
choices.why: The server parses the SQL, and its version decides which syntax exists.

choices.text: Staging has less memory than the laptop
choices.why: A lack of memory produces an out-of-memory error, never a syntax error.

prompt: What does a container image carry with the program?
hint: Draw the line at the kernel.

choices.text: Everything above the kernel: interpreter or compiler, libraries, configuration files
choices.why: Yes. The kernel is the one thing it does not bring; it uses the host's.

choices.text: Its own kernel, so it can boot anywhere
choices.why: That describes a virtual machine. A container uses the kernel of the machine it runs on.

choices.text: Only the program's own binary
choices.why: Then the libraries and the interpreter would still have to be installed on every machine, which is the problem containers solve.

choices.text: A copy of the host it was built on
choices.why: An image holds the files somebody chose for the program, not a snapshot of a machine.

prompt: Ana runs `docker run --rm golang:1.25 go version`. After the version is printed, what is left on her machine?

choices.text: Nothing at all: the image goes with the container
choices.why: `--rm` removes the container. The image stays, so the next run does not download it again.

choices.text: A stopped container and the image
choices.why: That is what the same command leaves without `--rm`.

choices.text: The image `golang:1.25` stays; the container is gone
choices.why: Right. The container was removed when `go version` ended; the image stays for next time.

choices.text: Go installed in `/usr/local/go`
choices.why: Nothing was installed on the host. The compiler lives in the image.

prompt: Which of these still depend on the machine a container runs on? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three things sit below the line the image draws, or outside it.

choices.text: The kernel
choices.why: Yes. Every container on the machine shares it.

choices.text: The processor architecture
choices.why: Yes. An image built for one architecture needs help to run on another; lesson 2 shows the error.

choices.text: The version of the libraries the program links against
choices.why: Those travel inside the image, at the versions somebody chose.

choices.text: Data written inside the container, once the container is removed
choices.why: Yes, in the sense that it is gone: it lived in the container's own layer. Lesson 7.

choices.text: The interpreter's version
choices.why: The interpreter is inside the image, which is the point of `golang:1.25` and `postgres:17`.

prompt: A virtual machine per project also ends the fight between PostgreSQL 16 and 17. What does it cost that a container does not?

choices.text: A licence for each copy of PostgreSQL running inside a VM
choices.why: PostgreSQL has no per-copy licence, in a VM or anywhere else.

choices.text: A whole operating system per project
choices.why: Right. A container shares the host's kernel and needs none of that.

choices.text: It cannot run two versions on one physical machine at once
choices.why: Two VMs can run on one machine; that is how it settles the fight.

choices.text: Network access between the two projects
choices.why: A VM has networking. The cost is elsewhere.

prompt: With PostgreSQL running in a container, Ana runs `ps -C postgres` on the host. What does she see?

choices.text: Nothing at all, because a container's processes are invisible to the host's tools
choices.why: The host saw six `postgres` processes, with ordinary numbers.

choices.text: One `containerd` process standing in for the database
choices.why: The database's own processes appear, under their own name.

choices.text: The postgres processes, with ordinary host process numbers
choices.why: Yes. A container is a process on the host, and the host lists it like any other.

choices.text: An error: `ps` needs `docker` to read a container
choices.why: `ps` reads the host's process table, where the container's processes already are.

prompt: On the host, Ana's `postgres` is process 10912. Read `/proc/1/status` from inside the container again: what process number does the same `postgres` have in there?
hint: The file's name already says it.

prompt: `docker top db` shows the database running as UID 999, and `id postgres` inside the container says 999 is `postgres`. Why might the host show a different name for 999, or none?
hint: Who turns a number into a name?

choices.text: Because the container's UID 999 is translated to a random host UID
choices.why: In this lab the number is the same on both sides; 999 is 999. Only the name lookup differs.

choices.text: Names come from each side's own `/etc/passwd`
choices.why: Right. The process is UID 999 everywhere; the name is a local lookup.

choices.text: Because PostgreSQL renames its user when it starts
choices.why: The name comes from the image's `/etc/passwd`, not from PostgreSQL at run time.

choices.text: Because `ps` cannot read processes owned by other users
choices.why: `ps` listed them; it simply has no name of its own for 999.

prompt: Bruno starts a container whose command converts one file and exits. One second later `docker ps` no longer lists it. What happened?
hint: How long does a container live?

choices.text: It crashed, because containers are meant to run forever
choices.why: Nothing says a container has to stay up; many do one job and stop.

choices.text: Docker removed it for using too much memory
choices.why: Nothing here hit a limit. A finished command is enough to explain it.

choices.text: It is still running, hidden from `docker ps`
choices.why: `docker ps` lists every running container; a stopped one needs `-a`.

choices.text: Its main process finished, so it stopped
choices.why: Right. A container lives as long as its main process; one that did its job and exited is done, not broken.

prompt: Match each mechanism to what it does for a container.
hint: One limits sight, one limits use, one supplies files.

pairs.right: Limit what the process can see: processes, hostname, network
Limit how much the process can use: memory, CPU, processes
Supply the filesystem the process sees

right_distractors: Boot a second kernel for the container

prompt: Ana writes `/note` in container `one`. Container `two` came from the same image. Why can `two` not read the file?

choices.text: Because `two` started before the file was written
choices.why: Order does not matter; `two` would not see it if it started afterwards either.

choices.text: Its write landed in `one`'s own layer
choices.why: Right. Containers never write into the image they share.

choices.text: Because Alpine forbids creating files in the root directory
choices.why: `one` wrote and read `/note` without trouble.

choices.text: `two` runs as another user
choices.why: Both run as root here; permissions are not what separates them.

prompt: `docker image ls` shows `alpine:3.22` with `CONTENT SIZE` 3.88MB and `DISK USAGE` 12.8MB. What explains the difference?
hint: One is how it travels, the other how it sits.

choices.text: Content size is compressed, as it travels from a registry; disk usage is unpacked on this disk
choices.why: Right. Layers travel compressed and are unpacked when pulled.

choices.text: Disk usage also counts the writable layers of every container ever started from this image on the machine
choices.why: Containers have their own column elsewhere; this is the image.

choices.text: Content size counts only the files Alpine changed since 3.21
choices.why: It counts the whole image, compressed.

choices.text: The two columns measure the same thing in different units
choices.why: Both are in MB, and they differ by more than three times.

prompt: Ana runs `docker rm -f one two db`. Which of these is still on her machine afterwards?

choices.text: The tables the database created
choices.why: They lived in `db`'s writable layer and went with it.

choices.text: The file `/note`
choices.why: It lived in `one`'s own layer, and `one` is gone.

choices.text: The image `alpine:3.22`
choices.why: Yes. Removing containers never removes the image they came from.

choices.text: The container `db`, stopped
choices.why: `-f` stops it and `rm` removes it.

prompt: Docker never changes an image when a container writes. Each container writes into its own ___ layer on top of it.
Match each word to what it names.

pairs.right: A read-only filesystem plus metadata, started from
An image's files, a writable layer and a running process
A server that stores images and hands them out
Storage that outlives the containers using it

prompt: A teammate says "the container has the new version now" after a deploy. In Docker's terms, what almost certainly happened?
hint: Can a running container's image change?

choices.text: The old container stopped and a new one started from the new image
choices.why: Right. A container keeps the image it was started from; a new version means a new container.

choices.text: The running container downloaded the new image into its writable layer
choices.why: A container does not swap its image. Its layer only holds what its own process writes.

choices.text: The image was edited in place while the container ran
choices.why: Images are read-only. A new version is a new image.

choices.text: The container rebooted its kernel with the new code
choices.why: There is no kernel of its own to reboot.

prompt: Put the life of Ana's database container in order.
hint: It starts from something that already exists.
items: The image `postgres:17` is on the machine
`docker run -d` creates a container from it and starts `postgres`
PostgreSQL writes its tables into the container's own layer
`docker rm -f` stops the container and removes it with its layer
The image is still there for the next container

prompt: Bruno argues that containers start in about the time their program takes to start. Which fact from this lesson supports him?
hint: What has to happen before the first line of the program runs?

choices.text: Images are compressed when they travel
choices.why: That makes a download faster, not a start.

choices.text: Each container gets its own writable layer
choices.why: True, but it is not what makes a start quick.

choices.text: Docker keeps the image after `--rm`
choices.why: That saves a download on the next run, not boot time.

choices.text: A container is a process on the host's kernel, so there is no operating system to boot
choices.why: Right. Starting a container is starting a process, with walls.
